messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{out,avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean output)
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (absolute maximum)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (peak-to-peak ripple 0.7-0.8s)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (cold start to 1.8V)
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability 0.6-0.8s)
    *   Piezo Characteristics:
        *   Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
        *   $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ peak at S1.
        *   Operating conditions S1-S6 vary $I_p, f, C_p, R_L$.
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, max 4 switches, max 2 SYNC controllers.

    *   FBR failed on:
        *   S2: ripple, startup, settled.
        *   S3: $V_{max}$ (too high, $4.2\text{ V} > 3.6\text{ V}$), settled.
        *   S4: $V_{avg}$ (too low), ripple, startup, settled.
        *   S5: $V_{avg}$ (too low), startup.
        *   S6: $V_{avg}$ (too low), startup.
    *   Main Issues with FBR:
        *   Efficiency is low due to diode drops (especially for low $I_p$ or high $R_L$).
        *   No voltage regulation (S3 exceeds 3.6V).
        *   Startup can be slow if the storage capacitor is too large or input current too low.

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* This is the gold standard for piezo. It uses an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage across the piezo capacitance $C_p$ at the voltage peaks, significantly increasing the energy extracted.
    *   *Synchronous Rectification:* Replacing diodes with switches to eliminate voltage drops.
    *   *Zener Clamping:* To prevent $V_{out} > 3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Parallel-SSHI or Basic SSHI)**
        *   Basic SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to invert $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks.
        *   Circuit: Piezo -> Bridge -> Storage. Adding an inversion loop (L and S) across the piezo.
        *   Or a simpler version: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Storage, and a switch/inductor circuit that triggers at the peak.
        *   Actually, the most effective is often a "Parallel-SSHI" or "Series-SSHI", but we have limited components. Let's try a basic SSHI structure.
        *   Structure: Piezo nodes (pzp, pzn). A bridge rectifier (D1-D4) converts to `out`. An inductor L1 and switch S1 connected across the piezo to invert charge.
        *   Wait, a simpler SSHI: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ `out`. Inductor L1 and switch S1 in parallel with the piezo. When the piezo voltage reaches a peak, S1 closes, transferring energy from $C_p$ to L1 and then back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity.

    *   **Design 2: Active Rectification (Synchronous)**
        *   Use switches instead of diodes to reduce $V_{drop}$.
        *   However, we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNC controllers. A full bridge needs 4 switches. 2 SYNC controllers can handle the timing.
        *   Actually, a "Half-Wave" Synchronous Rectifier might be simpler and more efficient for some conditions.

    *   **Design 3: FBR with Zener and Optimized Capacitor**
        *   The reference design failed $V_{max}$ on S3. A Zener diode (DZ33) on `out` will cap the voltage at 3.3V.
        *   But FBR failed $V_{avg}$ on S4, S5, S6. We need more power extraction.

    *   A common SSHI implementation:
        Piezo (pzp, pzn) is connected to a full-bridge (D1-D4).
        Then, an inductor L1 and switch S1 are connected from pzp to pzn (or pzp to ground, etc.).
        Wait, the standard SSHI: switch S1 and L1 are in parallel with the piezo.
        S1 closes when $|V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}|$ is max.
        $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.

    *   *Refining SSHI:*
        - Piezo nodes: pzp, pzn.
        - Bridge: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]. (Wait, this is a full bridge).
        - L-C Inverter: L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1.
        - G1: edges="both", phase=0.0 (triggers at peaks), $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{L \times 25\text{nF}}$.
        - Storage: C1 [out, 0].
        - Protection: D5 [0, out] (DZ33) to ensure $V_{out} \le 3.6\text{V}$.

    *   *Self-Correction on Bridge:*
        Full bridge is:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        Is this correct?
        If pzp is positive and pzn is negative:
        pzp -> out (D1 conducts)
        0 -> pzn (D4 conducts)
        If pzp is negative and pzn is positive:
        pzn -> out (D2 conducts)
        0 -> pzp (D3 conducts)
        Yes, that works.

    *   *Refining Active Rectification (Design 2):*
        Given the component limit and SYNC controllers, a full active bridge is hard.
        What if we use a Half-Bridge or a Charge Pump?
        Actually, let's try a "Synchronous Half-Wave Rectifier" with a capacitor.
        S1 [pzp, out], G1 (pos peak).
        This might be too inefficient.

    *   *Let's look at the failure of FBR again.*
        S4, S5, S6 failed $V_{avg}$ (1.8V).
        $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ (S1).
        At S4: $I_p = 25\text{uA}, f = 50\text{Hz}, C_p = 32.5\text{nF}$. $V_{oc} = 25\text{uA} / (2\pi \cdot 50 \cdot 32.5\text{nF}) \approx 2.45\text{V}$.
        With diode drops ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$ total for two DSCH diodes), $V_{out}$ will be around $2.45 - 0.5 = 1.95\text{V}$ peak. The average $V_{out}$ for a capacitor-buffered rectifier is close to the peak, but the load $R_L$ draws current.
        S4: $R_L = 1\text{M}\Omega$. Power needed at $1.8\text{V}$ is $1.8^2/1\text{M} = 3.24\mu\text{W}$.
        S5: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$. Power needed at $1.8\text{V}$ is $1.8^2/150\text{k} = 21.6\mu\text{W}$.
        S6: $R_L = 200\text{k}\Omega$. Power needed at $1.8\text{V}$ is $1.8^2/200\text{k} = 16.2\mu\text{W}$.
        The FBR is losing too much to diode drops.

    *   *Alternative: Synchronous Rectification (Simplified)*
        Instead of a full bridge, maybe a switch and a diode?
        Or, use the SYNC to only connect the piezo to the capacitor at the peaks?
        No, a standard SSHI is the way to increase the voltage.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener*
        - FBR (D1-D4, DSCH)
        - L1 and S1 for inversion (pzp -> n1 -> pzn)
        - G1 (SYNC, edges="both")
        - C1 (Storage)
        - D5 (DZ33 Zener)
        This increases the effective $V_{oc}$ by reducing the $C_p$ charge loss.

    *   *Design 2: Active Rectifier (S-Rect)*
        - S1 [pzp, out], G1 (pos peak)
        - S2 [pzn, out], G2 (neg peak)
        - D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn] (return paths)
        - C1 (Storage)
        - D5 (DZ33 Zener)
        This eliminates two diode drops.

    *   *Design 3: Boost-like SSHI*
        - L1 in series with the piezo? No, that's not how it works.
        - Let's try a "Synchronous Charge Extraction" (SCE) approach.
        - S1 [pzp, out], G1 (pos peak)
        - S2 [pzn, out], G2 (neg peak)
        - This is effectively what Design 2 does.

    *   *Wait, the SYNC controller:* "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
        This is perfect for SSHI.
        In SSHI, the switch S1 closes at the peak of $V_{pzp}$.
        If the bridge is present:
        When $V_{pzp}$ is max, the bridge is conducting.
        The inversion switch S1 connects pzp to pzn via L1.
        This flips the charge on $C_p$.
        $V_{pzp}$ goes from $+V_{max}$ to $-V_{max}$.
        Then the bridge conducts again in the opposite direction.

    *   *Let's refine Design 1 (SSHI):*
        - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        - D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
        - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn, ctrl: G1
        - G1: SYNC, edges="both", ton=... (to be optimized), phase=0.0
        - C1: out -> 0
        - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)

    *   *Let's refine Design 2 (Synchronous Bridge-ish):*
        - S1: pzp -> out, ctrl: G1 (edges="pos")
        - S2: pzn -> out, ctrl: G2 (edges="neg")
        - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        - C1: out -> 0
        - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        - G1: SYNC, edges="pos", ton=...
        - G2: SYNC, edges="neg", ton=...
        This replaces the two high-side diodes with switches.

    *   *Let's refine Design 3 (Modified SSHI - Series):*
        - Some SSHI versions use a capacitor $C_{fly}$ to store the flipped charge.
        - But we have limited components. Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" where the L-S circuit is across the piezo.
        - Let's try a design without the full bridge for the inversion part.
        - Actually, let's just try a very large storage capacitor for Design 3? No, the reference design already had 2.2uF.

    S3: $V_{max}$ was $4.2\text{V}$.
    S4, S5, S6: $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$.
    SSHI should significantly increase the voltage, and DZ33 will clamp it.

    Let's double check the SYNC timing for Design 1:
    $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    For $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}, t_{on} = 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = 3.14 \times 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
    The allowed $t_{on}$ is $1\mu\text{s}$ to $1\text{ms}$. $50\mu\text{s}$ is well within range.

    *Wait, I need to make sure the SYNC triggers at the correct time.*
    "closes its switches... at the piezo voltage extrema... which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
    This is exactly when the voltage is maximum.

    *Double Check Design 1 (SSHI) Connectivity:*
    Pzp, Pzn are the terminals.
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    L1: pzp -> n1
    S1: n1 -> pzn
    G1: SYNC (edges="both")
    C1: out -> 0
    D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    This uses 4 diodes, 1 inductor, 1 switch, 1 SYNC, 1 capacitor, 1 zener = 9 components.

    *Double Check Design 2 (Synchronous Rectifier):*
    S1: pzp -> out, G1 (pos)
    S2: pzn -> out, G2 (neg)
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    C1: out -> 0
    D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    This uses 2 switches, 2 SYNCs, 2 diodes, 1 capacitor, 1 zener = 8 components.

    *Let's consider a Design 3: an Improved FBR (Just for safety).*
    Maybe a different bridge? No, FBR is just a bridge.
    What about a Voltage Doubler?
    Piezoes are high impedance, so a charge pump/doubler can work.
    C1: pzp -> n1
    D1: n1 -> out
    D2: 0 -> n1
    ...
    No, SSHI is generally more robust.

    Let's go with:
    1.  SSHI (FBR + L-S inversion)
    2.  Synchronous Half-Bridge (S-Rect)
    3.  FBR + Zener (Simple but fixes $V_{max}$) -> Actually, let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" variant or a "Series-SSHI" variant.
        Actually, a "Standard SSHI" often has a capacitor $C_{fly}$ in the inversion path.
        Wait, the most basic SSHI *is* the one with the inductor. Let's try a variation of the L-S circuit.

    One more look at the S-Rect (Design 2):
    If $S1$ is closed, $V_{out} = V_{pzp}$.
    If $S2$ is closed, $V_{out} = V_{pzn}$.
    But we need the return path. D3 and D4 provide that.
    This removes the drop of D1 and D2.

    Wait, if I use a full bridge of switches?
    S1: pzp -> out, G1 (pos)
    S2: pzn -> out, G2 (neg)
    S3: 0 -> pzp, G1 (pos)
    S4: 0 -> pzn, G2 (neg)
    This would be a fully synchronous bridge.
    G1 (pos peak): S1 and S3 close.
    G2 (neg peak): S2 and S4 close.
    This removes all diode drops!

    *Revised Design 2 (Full Synchronous Bridge):*
    S1: pzp -> out, ctrl: G1
    S2: pzn -> out, ctrl: G2
    S3: 0 -> pzp, ctrl: G1
    S4: 0 -> pzn, ctrl: G2
    G1: SYNC, edges="pos", ton=...
    G2: SYNC, edges="neg", ton=...
    C1: out -> 0
    D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    This uses 4 switches, 2 SYNCs, 1 capacitor, 1 zener = 8 components.

    Let's refine the "Full Synchronous Bridge" (Design 2).
    Wait, if $S1$ and $S3$ are closed for $t_{on}$, it's just a pulse of current. A rectifier should be closed for the whole half-cycle.
    But the SYNC controller only closes for $t_{on}$ (max $1\text{ms}$).
    $1\text{ms}$ is way too short for a half-cycle ($100\text{Hz} \to 5\text{ms}$ half-cycle).
    So Design 2 (Full Synchronous Bridge) will NOT work as a rectifier. It will only work as a switched-capacitor converter.

    So Design 1 (SSHI) is the most promising because $t_{on}$ is *supposed* to be short ($\sim 50\mu\text{s}$).

    Let's rethink Design 2. If I can't do a synchronous bridge, how about a synchronous *boost* or *buck*? No, too complex.
    What if Design 2 is just an FBR with a very large storage capacitor and a Zener? No, the reference design already tried that.

    Let's try a different inversion circuit for Design 2.
    Instead of L-S, maybe a C-S (charge pump)?
    S1: pzp -> n1, G1 (pos)
    S2: n1 -> out, G2 (neg)
    This is a charge pump.

    Actually, let's try:
    Design 1: SSHI (FBR + L1 + S1 + G1)
    Design 2: SSHI with a different L-S configuration (S1: pzp -> n1, L1: n1 -> pzn) - Wait, that's the same.
    Design 2: FBR + DZ33 + a very small inductor in series with the piezo? No.

    Wait! What if Design 2 is a "Synchronous Rectifier" where the switches are used *not* as a bridge, but to bypass the diodes?
    No, the $t_{on}$ is the limiting factor.

    Let's try Design 2 as an SSHI but with a *different* bridge.
    What if we use DSCH for the bridge and just optimize the values?
    Actually, the reference design FBR already used DSCH.

    Let's try:
    Design 1: SSHI (FBR + L-S inversion)
    Design 2: A "half-wave" SSHI (Diodes and one L-S loop)
    Design 3: SSHI with a different SYNC configuration (e.g., phase shift).

    Wait, let's try a "Cold Start" optimized circuit.
    The problem is $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    A large capacitor $C_{out}$ slows down $t_{up}$ but reduces ripple.
    A small $C_{out}$ speeds up $t_{up}$ but increases ripple.
    The evolution strategy will optimize $C_{out}$.

    Let's double check the SSHI circuit one more time.
    The "Standard" SSHI:
    1.  Piezo is connected to a rectifier.
    2.  An inductor L and switch S are in parallel with the piezo.
    3.  S closes at the voltage peaks.
    This is exactly what I proposed for Design 1.

    What about Design 2?
    Maybe a "Series-SSHI"?
    In Series-SSHI, the inductor and switch are in series with the piezo.
    But that's more complex.

    Let's try a "Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor" with a capacitor (C-SSHI).
    Wait, let's just propose three variations of the L-S inversion.
    1.  L-S across piezo, Full Bridge.
    2.  L-S across piezo, but use a different Zener (or no Zener and see). No, DZ33 is needed for $V_{max}$.
    3.  L-S across piezo, but use only a half-bridge (to see if it's faster).

    Actually, a better Design 2:
    Instead of a full bridge, use a center-tapped transformer? No, we don't have one.
    How about a "Synchronous Charge Extraction" (SCE)?
    S1: pzp -> out, G1 (pos peak)
    S2: pzn -> out, G2 (neg peak)
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    This uses the switches to "dump" the piezo charge into the capacitor.
    With $t_{on} = 1\text{ms}$, it might actually work!
    Let's compare:
    SSHI: flips the voltage to *increase* the total charge extracted per cycle.
    SCE: just dumps the charge at the peak.
    Both are better than FBR.

    *Comparing SCE and SSHI:*
    SSHI is generally more powerful.
    Let's try:
    Design 1: SSHI (FBR + L-S inverter)
    Design 2: SCE (S1: pzp->out, S2: pzn->out, D3: 0->pzp, D4: 0->pzn)
    Design 3: FBR + Zener (as a baseline to see if the Zener alone fixes S3 and the optimizer fixes the rest).

    Let's refine Design 2 (SCE) again:
    S1: pzp -> out, ctrl: G1 (edges="pos")
    S2: pzn -> out, ctrl: G2 (edges="neg")
    D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
    D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    C1: out -> 0
    D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    G1: SYNC (edges="pos")
    G2: SYNC (edges="neg")
    This uses 2 switches, 2 SYNCs, 2 diodes, 1 cap, 1 zener = 8 components.

    Let's refine Design 1 (SSHI) again:
